passage:
The call came at ten, while Ramesh was checking copies in the staffroom of the village school. A man in a police uniform, a badge on the wall behind him. "A parcel in your name has illegal goods. You are under arrest on this call. Do not disconnect. Tell anyone, and your family will be charged too."
Ramesh's mouth went dry. He had never even been to the city post office.
They kept him on video for three hours. He moved to the empty science lab so no one would see. Every time he looked away, the man barked at him. To clear his name, he must transfer his savings to a verification account by afternoon.
He thought of his mother, of the shame if the village heard. He was typing his bank password when Sahil, the maths teacher, pushed open the lab door, saw his face, and said, "Ramesh? Who are you talking to?"

qa.q: How long did they keep Ramesh on video?
qa.a: They kept him on video for three hours.

qa.q: What was Ramesh afraid of during the call?
qa.a: He was afraid of arrest, of his mother being dragged in, and of the shame if the village heard.

qa.q: What should Ramesh do now that Sahil has opened the door?
qa.a: He should end the call, tell Sahil everything, call the police himself on an official number and report to the cybercrime helpline, since real police do not arrest people over video calls.

qa.q: What might Sahil notice when he sees Ramesh's face?
qa.a: Sahil likely sees fear and strain and guesses something is badly wrong, which is why he asks who Ramesh is talking to.

grounding: A young teacher is kept on a video call by fake police, ordered to keep it secret and pay to clear his name, and fear stops him thinking until Sahil walks in.

passage:
The caller said he was from the immigration office, and Bilal's stomach dropped. "Your student visa is linked to a fraud case. An officer will arrest you tonight unless you cooperate. Stay on this line. Speak to no one."
For ninety minutes Bilal sat on his bed in the Toronto flat, the phone hot against his ear. He answered questions about his bank, his family in Lahore, his part-time job. The voice switched between stern and almost kind: "We want to help you. Pay the security bond and we close the file."
He thought of his mother's face if he were sent home. His hands shook so hard he dropped his card.
The door clicked. His flatmate Hiroshi came in with groceries, saw him, and quietly held up his own phone screen: HANG UP. REAL OFFICERS DON'T DO THIS.
Bilal stared at the words, the voice still talking in his ear.

qa.q: How long did Bilal sit on his bed on the call?
qa.a: Bilal sat on his bed for ninety minutes.

qa.q: What was Bilal thinking about that made his hands shake?
qa.a: He was thinking of his mother's face if he were sent home, and the fear of arrest made his hands shake.

qa.q: What should Bilal do after reading Hiroshi's screen?
qa.a: He should hang up, contact the immigration office through its official number himself, and report the call, rather than paying any bond.

qa.q: How did Hiroshi respond on seeing Bilal?
qa.a: Hiroshi quietly broke the secrecy by holding up a message telling Bilal to hang up, showing care without frightening him further.

grounding: A student abroad is kept on a long call by a fake official who threatens arrest and demands secrecy and payment, until his flatmate steps in.

passage:
The power had gone out across the colony, the rain was hammering on the window, and Vaibhav's phone was at twelve percent when the video call came.
A man in a police uniform, an office behind him with a flag. "This is the customs crime branch. A parcel in your name contains illegal drugs. You are under digital arrest. Do not disconnect. Do not tell anyone. If you tell your family, they will also be charged."
Vaibhav's hands went cold. He'd done nothing. But the man had his name, his Aadhaar number, his address.
For two hours, they kept him on camera. "To clear your name, transfer your savings to our verification account. It will be returned after checking."
He was typing in the account number when someone pounded on his door. His friend Asif, soaked. "Your phone's been busy for hours, I got worried!"
Vaibhav turned the screen toward him. Asif took one look and pressed "end call." "Real police don't arrest people on video. Come, we're reporting this now."

qa.q: What did the man claim was in the parcel?
qa.a: Illegal drugs.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel during the two-hour call?
qa.a: Vaibhav felt terrified and trapped, his hands cold, afraid to disconnect or tell anyone.

qa.q: What did Asif do that stopped the scam?
qa.a: Asif ended the call, explained real police don't arrest people on video, and took Vaibhav to report it at once.

qa.q: How did the callers use secrecy against Vaibhav?
qa.a: They told him not to disconnect or tell his family, so fear and isolation would stop him thinking or asking anyone.

grounding: It shows an adult kept on a video call by fake officials claiming a crime, isolated by fear and secrecy until a friend breaks in.

passage:
On Friday afternoon, in his Gurgaon flat, Uday got a call from a man who said he was from a central investigation agency. Uday's bank account, the man said, had been used for money laundering. A "senior officer" joined on video, in uniform, with an official-looking seal.
"You will stay on camera. You will not contact anyone. This is a digital arrest."
Uday's mouth went dry. Could this really happen? He was just an accountant. They showed him a "warrant" with his name.
"Transfer ₹1.2 lakh to the government safe account. It will be returned after investigation."
He was so frightened that he did it.
When his flatmate Harish came home at eight, Uday was still sitting stiff on the sofa, the laptop open, not allowed to move. Harish saw the screen and shut the laptop.
"Uday. This is a scam. We're calling the cybercrime helpline, right now."
Uday started shaking. Then, finally, crying.

qa.q: How much did Uday transfer?
qa.a: ₹1.2 lakh.

qa.q: How did Uday feel during the call?
qa.a: Uday felt frightened and trapped, his mouth dry, unable to think clearly or contact anyone.

qa.q: What did Harish do when he came home?
qa.a: Harish shut the laptop, told Uday it was a scam, and called the cybercrime helpline right away.

qa.q: How did the fake officers keep Uday from getting help?
qa.a: They kept him on camera and forbade him to contact anyone, so fear and isolation stopped him from checking.

grounding: It shows an adult kept on a video call by fake officials, told to stay silent and pay, until a flatmate breaks the spell.

passage:
"Nandini, you've been on that video call in the meeting room for three hours. Are you okay?" Minakshi whispered through the door.
Nandini waved her away, pale. On the screen, a man in uniform said, "Who is that? You were told not to speak to anyone."
Minakshi slipped inside anyway and read the screen over her shoulder: "MUMBAI POLICE CYBER CELL. SUSPECT: NANDINI."
"They say a courier with fake passports was sent in my name," Nandini said, voice trembling. "I have to transfer my savings for verification or they'll arrest me today."
"Nandini. Real police don't arrest people on video calls. And they never ask for money to clear your name."
"But he has my ID number."
"Scammers buy those." Minakshi reached over and ended the call.
Nandini burst into tears. "I was so scared. They said if I told anyone, my parents would be arrested too."
"That's how they trap you. Come, let's call the cybercrime helpline together."

qa.q: How long had Nandini been on the video call?
qa.a: For three hours.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel during the call?
qa.a: Nandini felt terrified and pale, believing she would be arrested and her parents too if she told anyone.

qa.q: What did Minakshi do that helped?
qa.a: Minakshi came in anyway, explained real police don't arrest on video or ask for money, ended the call, and offered to call the cybercrime helpline together.

qa.q: How did the callers use fear and secrecy?
qa.a: They threatened arrest and said her parents would be arrested too, so she wouldn't tell anyone or stop to think.

grounding: It shows an adult kept on a video call by fake police, frightened and told not to speak to anyone, until a colleague steps in.

passage: It still makes my hands cold to think about it. Last month a call came from someone saying he was from customs: a parcel in my name, with fake passports inside, had been seized in Mumbai. Then a "police officer" in uniform came on video, a station behind him and a badge on the desk. He said I was under "digital arrest", that I must stay on camera, not leave the room and not tell anyone, or my family would be arrested too. For three hours I sat on my bed, nodding, sweating. When he said I could clear my name by transferring my savings to a "verification account", I actually opened my banking app. Then Siddharth, my flatmate, knocked, wanting the charger. I pointed at the phone. He looked at the screen and simply ended the call. I cried and cried. He sat with me, and we called the cybercrime helpline together. Nobody gets arrested over video. I, Swati, had only been frightened into silence.

qa.q: What did the caller say was inside the parcel?
qa.a: Fake passports.

qa.q: How did Swati feel during the three hours on camera?
qa.a: Swati felt terrified and trapped, sweating and nodding, too frightened by the threats to think or ask anyone.

qa.q: What should someone do if a caller claims a digital arrest?
qa.a: End the call, ring the agency's official number themselves, tell family, and report to the cybercrime helpline, as Siddharth and Swati did.

qa.q: What might Siddharth have been thinking when he saw the screen?
qa.a: Siddharth likely felt alarmed but clear-headed, seeing threats on a video call, and ended it at once instead of waiting.

grounding: Shows a person kept on a video call by fake officials claiming a parcel is linked to a crime and told to pay, with fear and secrecy stopping them from thinking.
